question: What practical advice does Julie Zhuo give new managers who are expected to carry out a vision they didn’t create?
expected_points: Examine whether you genuinely believe in the strategy rather than simply following orders.
If it doesn’t make sense, discuss it with your manager and work toward alignment.
Your own conviction helps you communicate the team’s purpose effectively.
evidence_quote: Wait, why are we doing this? Do I believe this strategy? Does it make sense or not?

answer.summary: Julie Zhuo advises new managers not to simply repeat orders: examine whether they believe in the strategy, discuss doubts with the people responsible, and break the proposal into specific assumptions so they can find points of agreement or influence the plan.

sections.heading: Check your own conviction
sections.content: Ask yourself why the work is being done and whether the strategy makes sense to you. Zhuo says managers need conviction to help their teams understand the purpose; merely parroting a vision passed down through the organization makes that harder.

sections.heading: Have a real dialogue
sections.content: If you think the idea is bad, raise it with your manager, CEO, or another relevant person rather than putting on a brave face or acting like a soldier taking orders. The conversation can give you new information about why others support the proposal, surface assumptions, and give you a chance to influence it. Work toward alignment on what you can genuinely believe.

sections.heading: Get specific about what you disagree with
sections.content: Instead of judging a proposal as wholly good or bad, break it into its component hypotheses and identify which ones you believe and which you doubt. Zhuo illustrates this with a hypothetical plan to put a lemonade stand on every block: a manager might object because they doubt the assumption that people want lemonade. Naming the disputed assumption makes the disagreement more specific and can help steer the project.

sections.heading: Treat conviction as consequential, not guaranteed
sections.content: Zhuo says it is difficult to hold and convey a vision effectively if you do not believe in it, and she says she cannot recall a project becoming wildly successful when a manager thought it was a bad idea. This is her experience, not a guarantee about what will happen to any particular project.

answer.summary: Julie advises new managers not to simply relay orders: examine whether they believe in the strategy, discuss concerns with leadership, and break disagreements into specific assumptions so they can understand, influence, and get aligned on the work.

sections.heading: Build your own conviction
sections.content: Even if you did not create the vision, do the work to understand why the organization is pursuing it and ask yourself whether the strategy makes sense. Do not just act like a soldier carrying out orders or parrot what was passed down: without genuine belief, it is hard to help your team see the purpose and hold the vision.

sections.heading: Talk through doubts and get specific
sections.content: If you do not believe in the plan, have a dialogue with your manager, CEO, or another relevant leader rather than putting on a brave face. You may learn new information or influence the project. Instead of treating the proposal as simply good or bad, break it into its underlying hypotheses: identify which ones you believe and the particular assumption you question. That can reveal what you do support and make any disagreement—and possible adjustments—more precise. Work toward alignment so you can genuinely believe in what you are doing.
